The first frequency row is used regardless of which frequency window the request time actually falls in. A trip with a peak/off-peak split in `frequencies.txt` — e.g. two rows for the same `trip_id`, `06:00-09:00 @600s` and `09:00-15:00 @1200s`, which is ordinary GTFS — will report the 06:00-09:00 window and a 10-minute headway for a 10:30 arrival. `startTime`, `endTime`, and `headway` are all wrong for any request outside the earliest window.

`serviceDate` (and the caller's effective time) is already in hand here, so the row whose `[start_time, end_time)` contains the requested time should be selected, falling back to the first row only when none matches. The same `freqs[0]` / `freqRows[0]` shortcut is repeated in `trip_for_vehicle_handler.go:120`, `arrival_and_departure_for_stop_handler.go:437`, and `arrivals_and_departures_for_stop_handler.go:502`, so a shared selector here would fix all of them at once.

Seeding every trip ID with `nil` *before* the batch query means a failed batch query is indistinguishable from "these trips have no frequencies". If `GetFrequenciesForTrips` returns an error, the code logs a warning and falls through with the map fully seeded, so `frequencyForEntry` finds `ok == true` for every trip, skips its fallback query, and returns `nil` — the whole response goes out as a 200 with `frequency: null` on every arrival and `status.frequency: null` throughout.

That contradicts the PR description's "strict error propagation (HTTP 500) for database failures during frequency lookups", and per CONTRIBUTING a non-`sql.ErrNoRows` DB error should go through `serverErrorResponse`. Moving the seeding loop into the `else` branch (so it only runs after a successful batch) would at least let the per-trip fallback take over; propagating the error is better still.

The same pattern is in `trips_for_location_handler.go:437-444` and `trips_for_route_handler.go:335-343`.

This assignment sits below the `CANCELED` early return at line 103, so a canceled frequency-based trip gets `status.frequency: null` while the enclosing entry (`TripDetails.Frequency`, `ArrivalAndDeparture.Frequency`, `TripsForRouteListEntry.Frequency`) still carries the frequency — the same trip reports two different answers in one response. Frequency is static schedule data and is just as valid for a canceled trip as `serviceDate` and `blockTripSequence`, both of which the code deliberately computes before that early return. Consider moving the lookup up next to `blockTripSequence` for the same reason.

`tripIDs` here is unbounded — it is every distinct trip serving this stop on the target date, which at a busy downtown stop can be well over a thousand. This is the only query in the handler whose bind-variable count scales with trip count (`GetScheduleForStopOnDate` binds route IDs, `GetTripsByBlockIDs` binds block IDs), and it now hard-fails the whole request with a 500 ("too many SQL variables") on exactly the stops most likely to be requested.

`queryInBatches` in `reference_utils.go:520` exists for this and is documented as staying under the oldest 999-variable limit so behavior doesn't depend on which SQLite the build links against:

```suggestion
		allFreqs, freqErr := queryInBatches(ctx, tripIDs, api.GtfsManager.GtfsDB.Queries.GetFrequenciesForTrips)
```

When `includeStatus` is true (the default), `BuildTripStatus` was already called at line 76 with a nil `freqMap`, which runs `GetFrequenciesForTrip(ctx, tripID)` for this same trip inside `frequencyForEntry`. This is a second identical round-trip on every request. Passing a one-entry `freqMap` seeded here (or reading `status.Frequency` back) removes the duplicate — minor, but this PR's stated goal is eliminating redundant frequency queries. The same duplication exists in `arrival_and_departure_for_stop_handler.go:436`.

`frequencyForEntry` always uses `freqs[0]` — the first frequency row for the trip — regardless of which window the request's `serviceDate`/effective time actually falls into. A trip with a peak/off-peak split in `frequencies.txt` (ordinary GTFS: e.g. `06:00-09:00@600s` and `09:00-15:00@1200s` for the same `trip_id`) will always report the `06:00-09:00` window and headway, even for a 10:30 request.

Legacy Java doesn't do this — `ArrivalAndDepartureServiceImpl` resolves the frequency entry whose `[start_time, end_time)` actually contains the query time (`isFrequencyBasedArrivalInRange`), never "just the first row." The wiki spec already says "the applicable headway window" for this field, so this isn't just undocumented — it contradicts what's already written.

Confirmed client impact: Wayfinder (`ArrivalDeparture.svelte`) and Android (`ArrivalInfo.kt`) both render this field directly as "every N min, from/until HH:MM" — riders would see the wrong window/headway for any multi-window frequency trip. Android's `ArrivalAdapters.kt` also uses `frequency.startTime` in a sentinel-detection heuristic that would compare against the wrong boundary.

The same unbounded-list issue applies to `trips_for_route_handler.go:338`, `trips_for_location_handler.go:440`, and `arrivals_and_departures_for_stop_handler.go:298`.

Separately: this near-identical batch-fetch-and-seed block (build trip IDs, seed `freqMap[id] = nil`, call `GetFrequenciesForTrips`, append by `TripID`) is duplicated across all four of those files, with inconsistent failure handling — this file returns a 500 on query failure, the other three log a warning and continue with an empty/partial map (see the next comment for why that's also a correctness bug in at least one of them). Worth consolidating into one shared helper so there's a single place to fix both the batching and the error policy.

The same pattern is in `trips_for_location_handler.go:438` and `trips_for_route_handler.go:336`.

This headway loop has no cap on iteration count or generated entries. An `exact_times=1` frequency block with a small headway over a long window (e.g. 30s headway across a 20-hour span) generates on the order of 2,400 synthetic `ScheduleStopTime` entries per trip at that stop, with no upper bound the way `GetStopsForLocation`-style endpoints cap their result size elsewhere. A few such trips serving one busy stop could make a single request allocate and sort tens of thousands of entries. Worth adding a sane cap (with a warning log when hit), especially since this expansion is being kept as intentional behavior rather than reverted to match Java.

`BuildTripStatus`/`BuildTripSchedule` failures here now call `api.serverErrorResponse` and abort the whole request for *any* error the function can return — not just the new frequency-lookup error this PR adds. Previously, any `BuildTripStatus` error (e.g. a transient DB hiccup elsewhere in the block-snapshot logic) degraded gracefully to `status: null`/`schedule: null` in a 200. That's a wider behavior change than the PR's stated goal of propagating frequency errors, and it's inconsistent with sibling handlers touched by this same PR — `trips_for_route_handler.go` and `arrival_and_departure_for_stop_handler.go` still log-and-continue (`status = nil`) on the identical `BuildTripStatus` error path. Worth confirming this scope expansion is intentional, and if so, applying it consistently rather than per-handler.

Reviewed against legacy Java (pinned at the SHA the wiki already cites) and the codebase's own conventions, alongside @aaronbrethorst's review and an independent `/code-review` pass. Most of CodeRabbit's earlier actionable comments on this PR (N+1 caching, division-by-zero guard, error propagation in several handlers, the routeDirection key-type refactor, missing doc comments) are already fixed in the current HEAD and don't need further action — I re-verified each against the code rather than trusting the stale comment text.

Two spec-conformance items came out of comparing against legacy Java source:

1. **Frequency window selection always picks the first `frequencies.txt` row for a trip, not the one matching the request time** (see inline comment on `frequencyForEntry`). Legacy Java resolves the time-matching `FrequencyEntry` per request; this PR's `frequencyForEntry`/`freqs[0]` shortcuts don't. This needs fixing — see inline comment.
2. **`schedule-for-stop` expanding `exact_times=1` trips into discrete `scheduleStopTimes`** deviates from legacy Java, which lumps all frequency trips (`exact_times` 0 or 1) into `scheduleFrequencies` undifferentiated. We've decided to keep this behavior — it's a defensible improvement (GTFS's `exact_times=1` semantics call for exact timetable-equivalent output, and schedule-for-stop's underlying Java bean has no `exactTimes` field to fall back on, unlike the `frequency` object elsewhere). This has been documented in the `maglev.wiki` `schedule-for-stop` page's Implementation Decisions section — no action needed here, just flagging so the intentional divergence is visible in-PR too.

The rest are correctness/consistency findings from combining @aaronbrethorst's review with an independent `/code-review medium` pass — each verified against current HEAD and confirmed still applicable.
